title: Democratic and market institutions are eroding across many countries while civic resistance and selective reform remain active counterforces
source_unit: Bertelsmann Stiftung, Bertelsmann Transformation Index 2026 Global Trends: Repression meets resistance
geography: 137 developing and transition countries assessed across political transformation, economic transformation, and governance

observations.period: 2026; global political-regime balance and transformation trajectory

regime_balance.value: 56% of countries assessed are now ruled autocratically, reversing the BTI 2006 balance in which democracies were 55%

hard_line.value: hard-line autocracies account for 38% of all countries assessed, and two-thirds of autocracies are highly repressive dictatorships or failing states

long_run.value: two-thirds of countries surveyed since 2006 score lower in political transformation than 20 years ago

boundary.value: BTI scores and classifications summarize expert assessments of transformation conditions; they are not direct measures of every resident's political experience or a causal model of regime change

observations.method: Bertelsmann Transformation Index comparative expert assessment of political transformation, economic transformation, and governance, with review period from February 1, 2023 to January 31, 2025.
observations.uncertainty: Expert-coded indices involve judgment, country comparability limits, review-period lag, and possible visibility differences across regimes.
observations.subgroup: Citizens, opposition groups, journalists, civil-society organizations, businesses, public institutions, and populations under democratic or authoritarian rule.
observations.counterinterpretation: A regime classification can hide important variation within countries, and formal institutional decline can coexist with local reform, social autonomy, or strong civic organization.

observations.period: 2026; elections, participation rights, and rule of law

denominator.unit: countries assessed by BTI 2026 political-transformation indicators

elections.value: in 80 countries, national elections were held in 2023 or 2024, but 54% of all countries assessed had elections that failed minimum democratic standards
elections.unit: countries and share by election-quality assessment

participation.value: countries denying fundamental political participation rights rose from about one-quarter in 2016 to around 40% in BTI 2026

rule_of_law.value: the decline is tied to weaker separation of powers, judicial independence, protection of civil rights, and prosecution of abuse of office

analytic_signal.value: elections can persist as formal events while voice, contestability, oversight, and legal recourse lose practical force

observations.method: BTI political-transformation assessment of election quality, political participation, expression, association, assembly, rule of law, and civil rights.
observations.uncertainty: Election-quality thresholds and expert assessments do not fully capture informal power, local participation, or political agency outside formal institutions.
observations.subgroup: Voters, opposition candidates, journalists, civil society, courts, minority groups, and people affected by restrictions on assembly, association, expression, or press freedom.
observations.counterinterpretation: Elections that fail minimum standards can still create openings for mobilization, elite turnover, institutional resistance, or later reform.

observations.period: 2026; governance capacity, economic transformation, and inequality

denominator.unit: countries assessed by BTI 2026 economic-transformation and governance indicators

recovery.value: the report finds no comprehensive economic recovery after the pandemic and inflation surge

patronage.value: in autocracies, state-economy entanglement in patronage networks undermines fair competition, property rights, and social equality

governance.value: concentration of power is associated with efficiency deficits, weakened consensus orientation, and less capable policy responses to structural and environmental pressures

analytic_signal.value: political concentration can redistribute economic opportunity and institutional capacity at the same time, linking regime form to market access and public problem-solving

observations.method: BTI comparative assessment of market economy principles, social justice, governance capacity, consensus building, and management of transformation.
observations.uncertainty: The index reports cross-country institutional patterns but does not identify the causal contribution of regime form to economic performance or inequality in each case.
observations.subgroup: Workers, firms, entrepreneurs, politically connected groups, excluded populations, public agencies, and communities facing environmental or economic pressure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some concentrated states can deliver selected policies quickly, while some democracies can experience gridlock, capture, or unequal competition.

denominator.unit: countries assessed by BTI 2026 political and governance indicators

decline.value: 28 of 137 countries declined by at least 0.25 points during the review period, while only about one in twelve governments achieved measurable progress
decline.unit: countries with reported BTI score change

resistance.value: protests, civil-society engagement, institutional resistance, and peaceful transfers in selected cases continue to challenge authoritarian overreach, corruption, and abuse of power

examples.value: BTI highlights cases including Brazil, Latvia, Taiwan, Moldova, Botswana, India, South Africa, Senegal, Sri Lanka, Poland, and Georgia as examples of electoral integrity efforts, institutional resistance, reform, or mobilization

open_test.value: join participation restrictions, information control, local service performance, economic inequality, civic organization, protest, repression, institutional checks, election quality, and later reform or exit without treating resistance as guaranteed democratization

observations.method: BTI global trend synthesis and country expert assessments of political, economic, and governance transformation.
observations.uncertainty: Documented resistance indicates openings and counterforces, not durable reform, reduced repression, or equal access to political change.
observations.subgroup: Civil society, opposition movements, institutional reformers, journalists, voters, courts, workers, firms, and people exposed to state repression.
observations.counterinterpretation: Protest can be suppressed, co-opted, or fragmented; institutional resistance can preserve formal checks without changing deeper power relations.

related_sources.claim: The Bertelsmann Stiftung publication page supplies the publication date, scope, description, and report metadata.
The BTI global dashboard supplies the comparative 137-country findings, regime balance, election quality, participation-rights, and resistance summaries.
The BTI project page documents the three transformation dimensions and the expert-assessment basis of the index.

boundary: This record adds a comparative political-institutional route from elections, participation rights, rule of law, governance capacity, market competition, and civic resistance through legitimacy, economic opportunity, public problem-solving, and geopolitical resilience. It uses expert-coded country comparisons and review-period synthesis, not respondent-level data, a causal regime model, a prediction of democratic transition, or proof that any one protest produces durable reform.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official BTI global report and global findings pages were reviewed for 137-country coverage, autocratic-democratic balance, election quality, participation rights, rule of law, economic transformation, governance capacity, score changes, and resistance examples.
